title: Glyphosate Exposure During Mid-Pregnancy Linked to Preterm Birth Risk
excerpt: An NYU Langone study of 1,450 women found that higher levels of the common weedkiller Roundup's active ingredient during midpregnancy raised the odds of spontaneous early labor.
body:
• Women with higher glyphosate levels in urine samples taken at 18–25 weeks of pregnancy were more likely to deliver before 37 weeks, according to a new NYU Langone study of 1,450 women.
  • The link was specific to spontaneous preterm labor and was not observed during early pregnancy or in medically induced deliveries.
  • Over 80 percent of Americans carry detectable glyphosate in their urine, and the herbicide is widely used across Indian agriculture despite government restrictions.

Pregnant women exposed to the herbicide glyphosate — the active ingredient in Roundup — during the middle months of pregnancy face a higher risk of going into spontaneous labor before 37 weeks, according to a study published July 14 in the journal Environmental Pollution. The research, led by NYU Langone Health, is one of the largest to examine glyphosate's effects on pregnancy outcomes in humans.

The study tracked 1,450 women enrolled in the Children's Health and Environment Study who planned to deliver at NYU Langone-affiliated hospitals in New York City between 2016 and 2019. Each participant provided urine samples at two points: once between 4 and 17 weeks of pregnancy, and again between 18 and 25 weeks.

What the Data Shows

Women with higher concentrations of glyphosate in their midpregnancy urine samples were significantly more likely to experience spontaneous preterm birth. The pattern did not appear when glyphosate was measured during the first trimester, and there was no association with medically induced early deliveries — those prompted by conditions like preeclampsia or poor fetal growth.

"Our findings add to a growing body of evidence that exposure to glyphosate early in life may lead to health concerns that can echo throughout a lifetime."

— Teresa Herrera, MPH, lead author, NYU Grossman School of Medicine

The timing distinction is significant. Laboratory research in animals and cells has suggested that glyphosate may trigger inflammatory mechanisms capable of initiating labor. By separating spontaneous from medically induced preterm births, the NYU team found the herbicide's effects aligned more closely with inflammation-driven pathways than with complications that lead clinicians to intervene, according to the study published in Environmental Pollution.

A Chemical That's Everywhere

Glyphosate is the world's most widely used herbicide. It is sprayed on commercial crops including grains and legumes, and residues have been detected in cereals, snack foods, and fresh produce. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that more than 80 percent of Americans carry detectable levels of the chemical in their urine.

Past research has linked heavy occupational exposure — particularly among farmworkers — to non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other health problems, but less is understood about the effects of low-level, everyday exposure through food.

"These results underscore the need for stronger regulations to protect the health of pregnant women and infants, two groups long known to be especially vulnerable to chemicals in the environment," said senior author Leonardo Trasande, MD, a professor of pediatrics and population health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. He noted that organic farming methods can produce competitive yields, challenging the assumption that weed control must come at a health cost.

India's Complicated Relationship With Glyphosate

The findings carry particular weight for the Indian diaspora. Glyphosate is the second most consumed herbicide in India and is widely used in tea plantations across West Bengal and Assam, as well as on sugarcane, maize, and fruit crops. Despite being approved only for tea plantations and non-cropped areas, a bulletin from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research found that glyphosate formulations are used across at least 22 Indian states on food crops including cereals, pulses, vegetables, and spices.

India's Agriculture Ministry restricted glyphosate use in 2022, requiring application only through licensed pest control operators. Several states, including Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Kerala, and Telangana, have imposed additional restrictions or attempted outright bans. But implementation remains patchy — an April 2026 government meeting acknowledged there are not enough licensed operators to enforce the rules, and the Registration Committee is conducting a fresh review of the restrictions.

For diaspora families, the concern extends in both directions: glyphosate residues are present in the U.S. food supply, while imported Indian food products may carry traces from fields where the herbicide is used beyond its approved scope.

What's Next

The NYU researchers cautioned that their study cannot prove glyphosate directly causes preterm birth. They plan to investigate the biological mechanisms through which the herbicide may affect fetal development.

Lead author Herrera advised that families concerned about herbicide exposure may want to choose organic grains and produce when possible, while noting that the chemical is so widespread in the environment that individual dietary choices alone are unlikely to eliminate exposure entirely.

Preterm birth remains a leading cause of illness and death among newborns worldwide, with premature babies facing elevated risks of breathing problems, infections, and long-term developmental challenges. The study adds to mounting pressure on regulators — in the U.S., India, and globally — to reassess the safety thresholds for a chemical that most people unknowingly consume every day.
